analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 3.8% Medicare tax on investment income of high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out a provision of the 2010 health care law that imposes a 3.8% Medicare tax on investment income—things like interest, dividends, rents, royalties, and profits from selling stocks or property—but only for people with incomes above $200,000 ($250,000 for couples). Repealing it would mean high earners keep that money, and Medicare would collect less. The bill was introduced by one representative, never attracted a single cosponsor, and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers with adjusted gross incomes above $200,000 ($250,000 for joint returns) who earn substantial investment income would keep the 3.8% they would otherwise owe on interest, dividends, rents, royalties, and capital gains starting in 2013.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'unearned income Medicare contribution,' which since 2013 applies a 3.8% tax to net investment income—interest, dividends, annuities, royalties, rents, passive income, and gains from selling nonbusiness property.
Because the tax only applies to taxpayers with adjusted gross incomes of $200,000 ($250,000 for joint returns) or more, repeal delivers its benefit exclusively to upper-income households.
Restores the Internal Revenue Code as if the provision had never been enacted, eliminating the tax entirely rather than adjusting its rate or thresholds.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare would lose the revenue the tax was projected to raise, weakening the program's financing; and since the tax falls only on the top slice of earners, ordinary wage earners would see no tax relief from repeal.

drawbacks.text: The tax exists to shore up Medicare financing as part of the 2010 health care law; repealing it removes a dedicated revenue stream for the program without replacing it.
Every dollar of the benefit goes to households above the $200,000/$250,000 income thresholds, so no middle- or working-class taxpayer gains anything from repeal.

Supporters of such repeals have argued the tax penalizes saving and investment and adds complexity—but this bill offered no offsetting way to keep Medicare whole, so the funding loss was not addressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's entire benefit is a tax cut for households earning over $200,000–$250,000, paid for by shrinking Medicare's revenue. For ordinary working people there is no upside in the bill itself; the cost—a weaker Medicare trust fund—is diffuse but real. This is a straightforward transfer toward the top of the income distribution.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when this Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Adrian Smith introduced the bill on September 29, 2010, to repeal the 3.8% Medicare tax on high earners' investment income.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which is where tax bills start.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the last entry in the bill's history is the referral, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare's financing stayed intact and high earners continued to owe the investment-income tax; nobody gained from the bill's failure beyond the status quo holding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare funding and current tax law

for.name: Rep. Adrian Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the investment-income Medicare tax and it was referred to committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never took the bill up before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never progressed far enough to produce votes; it was a one-sponsor Republican bill with zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan alignment can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill's sole benefit is eliminating a 3.8% tax on interest, dividends, rents, royalties, and capital gains for households earning above $200,000/$250,000. The money would otherwise flow to Medicare, so their gain is Medicare's loss.
The tax is a dedicated Medicare revenue stream created by the 2010 health care law; repeal would have removed it without a replacement, weakening the program's finances for everyone who relies on it.
